items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: Imagine you started with 64 blue squares, and in any second there was a one in four chance of each of them changing colour. In the first second, 16 would change colour, leaving 48 blue squares. In the next second, a quarter of these change colour, but that's only 12; this leaves 36 blue ones. In the third second, nine would change colour, and so on. The rate of change falls as the number (concentration) of blue squares falls.

items.label: text
items.text: NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g) Heat is needed for this reaction to occur

items.label: text
items.text: white solidcolourless gases

items.label: text
items.text: These gases recombine further up the tube, where it is cooler, to form a white solid:

items.label: text
items.text: NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s) Heat is released from this reaction colourless gases white solid

items.label: text
items.text: The reaction reverses when the conditions are changed from hot to cool.

items.label: text
items.text: This can, again, be shown with the reversible arrow:

items.label: text
items.text: NH3(g) + HCl(g) = NH4Cl(s)

items.text: CHEMISTRY ONLY

items.label: section_header
items.text: REVERSIBLE REACTIONS IN A SEALED CONTAINER

items.label: text
items.text: A sealed container means that no substances are added to the reaction mixture and no substances escape from it. On the other hand, heat may be either given off or absorbed.

items.label: text
items.text: Imagine a substance that can exist in two forms, one of which we'll represent by a blue square and the other by a yellow square. Suppose you start off with a sample which is entirely blue.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 21.3 Blue squares converting to yellow ones

items.label: text
items.text: Because you are starting with a high concentration of blue squares, at the beginning of the reaction the rate at which they turn yellow will be relatively high in terms of the number of squares changing colour per second. The number of blue squares changing colour per second (the rate of change) will fall as the blue gradually gets used up.

items.label: text
items.text: But the yellow squares can also change back to blue ones again. This is because it is a reversible reaction, in which the products can react with each other and go back to form reactants. At the start, there aren't any yellow squares, so the rate of change from yellow into blue is zero. As their number increases, the rate at which yellow change to blue also increases.
